lead: This unit moves from the total station to satellite, laser and drone methods. You learn how each instrument measures, what errors limit it, and how to choose a method for a field job. After the unit you can compute coordinates from total station and GNSS data, judge satellite geometry, plan a drone or LiDAR survey, and set out simple construction and hydrographic work.
about: The unit covers modern field instruments and the geospatial data they produce. Chapter 5.1 explains the total station: components, working, errors, traversing and topographic use. Chapter 5.2 builds the GNSS principle from satellite signals to pseudorange, DGPS and RTK, with receivers and other constellations. Chapter 5.3 shows why satellite geometry and DOP control accuracy. Chapter 5.4 introduces LiDAR and laser scanning as time-of-flight point clouds. Chapter 5.5 applies drones: types, payloads, GSD, overlap, structure-from-motion and Indian rules. Chapter 5.6 sets out construction points from control, and Chapter 5.7 covers bathymetry and underground transfer. The order moves from ground instruments to satellite, airborne and specialist surveys, with cross-links to control, levelling and GIS.

chapters.idea: A total station combines an electronic theodolite, an EDM and a processor to measure angles and distances and compute coordinates at one setup.
chapters.depth: Cover the total station as an integrated electronic theodolite plus EDM plus processor. Components: EDM unit, horizontal and vertical angle encoders, telescope, processor, display, keypad, battery, storage, tribrach, optical or laser plummet, reflector prism and prism constant. Working: setup and levelling, centring, backsight orientation, angle and distance measurement, coordinate computation, stakeout, data transfer. Some syllabi call this an electronic tacheometer. Include motorized and robotic total stations in one line: motorized turns under keypad control, robotic follows a prism and can be run by one person. Field procedures: traverse, topographic detail, as-built, setting out; EDM without prism for short ranges; prism constant and atmospheric correction. Errors: instrument collimation, vertical index, circle eccentricity, prism constant, centring, height of instrument, target height, atmosphere, refraction, booking. Applications: cadastral, construction, roads, tunnels, monitoring. Keep depth at components-working-errors-applications; no wave physics of EDM.

figure.title: Total station signal and data path
figure.aria: Block diagram showing the EDM unit sending a beam to a reflector prism and returning, with angle sensors and distance feeding a processor that sends coordinates to display and storage.

chapters.example: At station P (E 1000.000 m, N 2000.000 m), backsight Q has azimuth 30°00′00″. A total station reads a clockwise horizontal angle of 75°30′00″ from PQ to R, a slope distance of 120.000 m and a zenith angle of 85°00′00″. Find the horizontal distance PR, the azimuth of PR, and the coordinates of R. Answer: d = 120 sin 85° = 119.543 m; azimuth PR = 105°30′00″; ΔE = 115.196 m, ΔN = −31.947 m; R = (1115.196 m, 1968.053 m).
chapters.trap: Using slope distance as horizontal distance, or forgetting the prism constant and target height.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 EDM; Unit 4 theodolite and traversing.
chapters.leave: EDM wave physics to Unit 1; traverse adjustment to Unit 2; curve setting out to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: GNSS finds a receiver position from the travel times of signals from several satellites whose positions are known.
chapters.depth: Cover GPS and GNSS: space segment with satellites, control segment with master control and monitor stations, user segment with receivers. Signals: carrier, code, navigation message; pseudorange and carrier-phase observation; broadcast ephemeris. Positioning methods: absolute single-point, relative DGPS, RTK, network RTK; static, fast static, kinematic; code versus phase. Receivers: antenna, channels, accuracy classes; GNSS versus GPS. Coordinates: WGS84 and UTM as the working frame; mention datum transformation but leave projection maths to Unit 1 and Unit 7. Errors list: satellite clock, ephemeris, ionosphere, troposphere, multipath, receiver noise; correction methods. Other constellations: GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, NavIC; GPS modernization. Some syllabi call this satellite positioning. Depth: principle, methods, receivers, errors, applications; leave DOP to 5.3.

figure.aria: Tree of GNSS positioning methods: absolute single-receiver SPP, and relative methods DGPS and RTK.

chapters.example: A GNSS receiver clock is ahead by 10 µs. It measures pseudoranges 20,200,000.000 m, 21,000,000.000 m, 19,800,000.000 m and 22,500,000.000 m. Take c = 299,792,458 m/s. Find the common range error and the corrected pseudoranges. Answer: error = c × 10 µs = 2997.925 m; corrected ranges are 20,197,002.075 m, 20,997,002.075 m, 19,797,002.075 m and 22,497,002.075 m.
chapters.trap: Assuming three satellites are enough; four are needed because the receiver clock bias is a fourth unknown.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 datums and coordinate systems; Unit 4 control surveys.
chapters.leave: DOP and accuracy to 5.3; map projections to Unit 1 and Unit 7.

chapters.idea: The spread of satellites in the sky, measured by DOP, sets how much range error becomes position error.
chapters.depth: Satellite geometry: elevation, azimuth, skyplot, satellite distribution. DOP family: GDOP, PDOP, HDOP, VDOP, TDOP; relation σ_position = DOP × σ_range. Accuracy measures: RMS, CEP, 2DRMS, confidence; separate precision from accuracy. Error sources in observations: ionosphere, troposphere, multipath, clock, ephemeris, user dynamics; which DOP does not fix. Satellite geometry and accuracy measures for planning: mask angle, observation window, mission planning. Other satellite navigation systems and GPS modernization in relation to geometry. Some syllabi call this DOP analysis. Depth: compute simple DOP, read a skyplot, state accuracy measures; leave full GNSS principle to 5.2.

figure.aria: Skyplot graph with a receiver linked to four spread satellites and to one satellite in a poor common direction.

chapters.example: Two satellites are used in a 2D fix. From receiver R at (0,0), satellite A is at (0,10000) m and satellite B is at (10000,0) m. The unit vectors to A and B are (0,1) and (1,0). Form H and compute HDOP. What happens if B is at (0,20000) m instead? Answer: H = [[0,1],[1,0]], HᵀH = I, HDOP = √2 = 1.414. If both unit vectors are (0,1), HᵀH is singular and HDOP is infinite.
chapters.trap: Treating high elevation as good geometry; DOP depends on angular spread, not signal strength.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 GNSS principle; Unit 4 weights and adjustment.
chapters.leave: Full error correction to 5.2; GIS overlay to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: LiDAR measures range from the two-way travel time of a laser pulse and builds a 3D point cloud by scanning.
chapters.depth: LiDAR: light detection and ranging. Time-of-flight range R = c t / 2. Types: airborne, terrestrial laser scanning, mobile mapping; discrete return, waveform, intensity. Components: laser, scanner mirror, detector, timer, GNSS and IMU for georeferencing. Working: scan pattern, multiple returns, point cloud, classification, DEM and DSM, canopy and bare earth. Errors: timing, angular, range, IMU and GNSS, scan geometry, reflectance, atmosphere. Applications: terrain, power lines, forestry, buildings, as-built, corridor mapping. Some syllabi call this laser scanning. Keep conceptual, no waveform processing maths.

figure.title: Time-of-flight laser scanning
figure.aria: Block diagram of a LiDAR scanner: laser pulse deflected by a mirror to a target, return detected, timed, and converted to a point cloud.

chapters.example: A LiDAR pulse returns after 2.00 µs. The scanner steps by 0.100° between pulses. Take c = 299,792,458 m/s. Find the range and the point spacing on a surface perpendicular to the beam at that range. Answer: R = c t / 2 = 299.792 m; step = 0.100° = 0.001745 rad; spacing = R × step = 0.523 m.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the divide by 2 in R = c t / 2, or treating intensity as elevation.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6 remote sensing basics; 5.2 GNSS and IMU.
chapters.leave: Image classification to Unit 6; point cloud GIS analysis to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A drone survey turns overlapping photographs and their positions into maps and elevation models through flight planning and structure-from-motion.
chapters.depth: UAV and drone surveying: types multirotor and fixed-wing; payload RGB, multispectral, LiDAR; flight planning: GSD, along-track and side overlap, altitude, ground control points, GNSS and RTK. SfM: matching common points, camera calibration, tie points, bundle adjustment, dense cloud; orthomosaic and DEM as products; image overlap. DGCA rules in India: permits, zones, pilot requirements in outline only. Applications: topographic mapping, construction monitoring, landslide and flood mapping, agriculture. Some syllabi call this drone photogrammetry. Depth: types, payloads, GSD and overlap, SfM concept, products; no full photogrammetry maths.

figure.title: Drone survey pipeline
figure.aria: Flow from flight planning through image capture and structure-from-motion to an orthomosaic and a digital elevation model.

chapters.example: A drone camera has pixel size 2.4 µm and focal length 8.8 mm. It flies at 120 m above ground. Find GSD. For a 3.0 km strip and a 150 m along-track footprint with 80% overlap, find the number of images. Answer: GSD = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ × 120 / 0.0088 = 0.0327 m = 3.27 cm; spacing = 150 × 0.20 = 30 m; images = 3000 / 30 + 1 = 101.
chapters.trap: Confusing GSD with contour interval, or using height above sea level instead of above ground.
chapters.leave: Photogrammetry equations to Unit 6; GIS analysis to Unit 7; detailed drone law beyond DGCA outline.

chapters.idea: Setting out reverses a survey: it places a designed point on the ground from known control coordinates.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Setting out: from control coordinates to pegs, angles and distances; horizontal and vertical control; reference lines; total station stakeout; GNSS stakeout; as-built check; tolerances. Construction surveys: site clearing, foundation, columns, road centreline, drainage, monitoring. Use coordinate method and angle-distance method. Keep short: one worked coordinate setting-out, one figure. Some syllabi call this setting out or layout surveying. Depth: construction setting out only; no structural design.

figure.title: Setting out a point
figure.aria: Flow for setting out: known control, instrument setup, computed azimuth and distance, peg marking, and as-built check.

chapters.example: Control station A is at (E 1000.000 m, N 1000.000 m) with backsight azimuth 0°00′00″. A building corner C is to be set at (E 1025.000 m, N 1040.000 m). Find the setting-out angle from the backsight and the horizontal distance AC. Answer: ΔE = 25.000 m, ΔN = 40.000 m; AC = √(25² + 40²) = 47.170 m; azimuth = atan2(25,40) = 32°00′19″.
chapters.trap: Using magnetic bearing instead of grid azimuth, or swapping easting and northing in atan2.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 total station; Unit 4 control and curves.
chapters.leave: Structural design; mass haul; detailed machine control.

chapters.idea: Hydrographic and underground surveys extend control and depth measurement to water and below the surface.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Hydrographic: bathymetry, echo sounder, two-way time, sound speed, tide reduction to chart datum, position fixing, sounding plan, chart. Underground: surface control, shaft transfer of coordinates and azimuth, underground traverse, tunnel alignment, breakthrough error. Keep short: depth and position, one bathymetry example, one underground transfer sketch. Some syllabi call this hydrographic surveying and mine surveying. Leave legal charting and mine design.

figure.title: Depth and underground survey flow
figure.aria: Two linked flows: surface control to echo sounder, tide reduction, and chart; surface control to shaft transfer and underground traverse.

chapters.example: An echo sounder records a two-way travel time of 0.040 s. Sound speed in water is 1500 m/s. The tide is 1.20 m above chart datum. Find the depth below the water surface and the reduced depth below chart datum. Answer: depth = 1500 × 0.040 / 2 = 30.0 m; reduced depth = 30.0 + 1.20 = 31.2 m.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the two-way divide by 2, or applying tide with the wrong sign.
chapters.leave: Tidal analysis; mine design; legal charting.
